blocks.text: Reading about Spring is not the same as building with it. In this Part you build a small but realistic service, **Library API**, in which librarians manage authors and books and members borrow and return copies. It is deliberately small enough to type in an afternoon, yet it uses the pieces a hiring manager expects to see: layered architecture, DTO records, Bean Validation, Spring Data JPA with relationships, a transactional business rule, `ProblemDetail` errors, role-based security, tests and a Docker Compose run.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The listings in this Part are written to compile against Spring Boot 3.5.x and to carry over to Boot 4 with the small changes noted in the text. They could not be executed while this guide was written, so type them in, run `./mvnw verify`, and fix typos as you go; the structure is what matters. Any output shown is typical, not captured.

### Requirements

- Librarians create and edit authors and books and see all loans.
- Anyone can browse authors and books (search by title, paged).
- A member who is logged in can borrow a book if a copy is available and can list their own loans.
- A librarian records the return of a loan.
- A book that has loans cannot be deleted; a book with no free copy cannot be borrowed; the ISBN is unique.

### Endpoints

### Package layout

Package by layer, which is the simplest to follow at this size (larger systems often package by feature instead).

**Project layout**

blocks.code:
library-api/
  pom.xml  Dockerfile  docker-compose.yml
  src/main/java/com/example/library/
    LibraryApplication.java
    domain/    Author  Book  Loan
    repository/ AuthorRepository  BookRepository  LoanRepository
    service/   AuthorService  BookService  LoanService
    web/       AuthorController  BookController  LoanController
               dto/ (records)   ApiExceptionHandler
    error/     NotFoundException  ConflictException
    config/    SecurityConfig  SecurityProps
  src/main/resources/
    application.yml
    db/migration/V1__init.sql
  src/test/java/com/example/library/
    web/BookControllerTest   service/LoanServiceTest

blocks.text:
The dependency rule is one-directional: `web` calls `service`, `service` calls `repository`, and nothing calls upwards. Entities stay inside `domain` and `service`; controllers only see DTO records.

blocks.text: The parent's dependency management supplies the version of every dependency above, so no `<version>` tags appear. There is no H2 dependency on purpose: repository-level tests use the same PostgreSQL via Testcontainers in a real project (see the testing chapter), and here we keep the test suite to unit and web-slice tests that need no database.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Spring Boot 4 split many starters. The web starter is now `spring-boot-starter-webmvc`, Flyway needs `spring-boot-starter-flyway`, and each technology has a matching `-test` starter. The simplest way to port: generate a project at start.spring.io with the same choices on the Boot 4 line and copy its dependency list. Application code in this Part is unaffected, apart from import packages for test-slice annotations.
### Configuration and schema

blocks.code:
spring:
  application:
    name: library-api
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/library}
    username: ${DB_USER:library}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD:library}
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
    open-in-view: false
  flyway:
    enabled: true

server:
  shutdown: graceful

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true

library:
  security:
    librarian-password: ${LIBRARIAN_PASSWORD:librarian-dev}
    member-password: ${MEMBER_PASSWORD:member-dev}
blocks.title: application.yml

blocks.text: `${NAME:default}` reads an environment variable with a fallback, so local runs work with no setup while Compose or production override the values from outside. Flyway runs the SQL migration at start-up and Hibernate only validates that the entities match it:

blocks.title: V1__init.sql

blocks.text: Save it as `src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__init.sql`. The file name matters: `V`, version, two underscores, description. Never edit a migration that has run anywhere; add `V2__...` instead.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Write requirements and an endpoint table first; it becomes your test checklist.
- Package by layer here, with one-way dependencies from web to service to repository.
- Flyway owns the schema, Hibernate only validates it, and configuration comes from environment variables with dev defaults.
- Never edit an applied migration.

This chapter builds everything below the web layer: three entities, three repositories, the services and the error types.

### Errors first

Two small exceptions express the business outcomes the web layer will translate to 404 and 409:

blocks.title: NotFoundException.java
ConflictException.java

blocks.text:
Both are unchecked, which matters for `@Transactional`: a `RuntimeException` leaving a transactional method rolls the transaction back by default.

### Entities

blocks.title: Author.java
Book.java
Loan.java

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- Fields have no setters; state changes go through behaviour (`checkOut`, `checkIn`, `markReturned`). The rule "you cannot borrow when no copy is free" lives in the entity, so it cannot be bypassed by a careless caller.
- Every association is `LAZY`. `@ManyToOne` defaults to `EAGER`, which is the usual cause of N+1 surprises, so we state it explicitly.
- `@Version` turns on optimistic locking. Two members borrowing the last copy at the same moment both read `copiesAvailable = 1`; the second `UPDATE` finds the version changed and fails with `ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException`, which we map to 409.
- Camel-case fields map to snake-case columns (`copiesTotal` to `copies_total`) through Spring Boot's default naming strategy.

### Repositories

blocks.title: BookRepository.java
LoanRepository.java

blocks.text:
in the same package. The `@EntityGraph` annotations tell Spring Data to join-fetch the author (and book) in the same query that loads the page. Without them, mapping 20 books to DTOs would trigger one extra query per book for `getAuthor().getName()`: the N+1 problem from the relationships chapter.

### Request and response records

DTOs are records. Validation annotations on the request records are what `@Valid` in the controller will check:

blocks.title: BookRequest.java
BookResponse.java

blocks.text: The other DTOs follow the same pattern and are one line each (shown together here; put each record in its own file):

blocks.title: OtherDtos.java

blocks.text:
From here on we use them as nested types of `OtherDtos` (`OtherDtos.LoanRequest`); in your own project, separate files are tidier. `PageResponse` exists because serialising Spring Data's `PageImpl` directly produces an unstable JSON shape that Spring warns against.

### Services

blocks.title: BookService.java

blocks.text:
Class-level `readOnly = true` is the default for the reads, and the three write methods override it with plain `@Transactional`. Note `update` never calls `save`: the entity is managed inside the transaction, so Hibernate notices the change and issues the `UPDATE` at commit (dirty checking). `PUT` here updates title, ISBN and author; copy counts change only through borrowing and returning.

`AuthorService` is the same shape (`list`, `get`, `create`) and is left as an exercise; its controller appears in the next chapter. The service that carries the real business rule is next:

blocks.title: LoanService.java

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `borrow` changes two rows (the book's counter and a new loan) in one transaction: both happen or neither does. If `checkOut` throws, nothing is saved.
- `Clock` is injected, not `LocalDate.now()` called blindly. Production gets the system clock; tests pass `Clock.fixed(...)` and assert exact due dates.
- The borrower name is a parameter, not read from a security context inside the service. The controller will pass the authenticated user's name; the service stays free of web and security types and is easy to unit test.
- Provide the clock bean once, in the main class:

blocks.title: LibraryApplication.java
Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you prevent two users from borrowing the last copy at the same time? Add optimistic locking with a `@Version` field. Both transactions read the same version; the first commit increments it, and the second commit's `UPDATE ...` `WHERE version = ?` matches zero rows, so Hibernate throws an optimistic-locking exception, which the API maps to 409 and the client can retry. The alternative is pessimistic locking (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), which blocks instead of failing and costs throughput under contention.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Put business rules in the domain and service layer, behind small, behaviour-named methods.
- Mark associations `LAZY` explicitly and fetch what you need with `@EntityGraph`.
- `@Transactional` on the service defines the unit of work; unchecked exceptions roll it back.
- `@Version` gives cheap protection against lost updates.
- Inject `Clock` for time-dependent logic so tests are deterministic.

sections.title: REST layer with validation and error handling

blocks.text:
The web layer should be thin: translate HTTP into a service call, and the result back into HTTP. No business rules, no entities, no repository calls.

### Controllers

blocks.title: BookController.java
LoanController.java

blocks.text:
`AuthorController` follows the `BookController` pattern with `GET /api/authors`, `GET /api/authors/{id}` and `POST` `/api/authors` over a small `AuthorService`; write it as practice. Three things to notice in the two controllers above:

- `@Valid` on the `@RequestBody` runs Bean Validation before the method body; invalid input never reaches the service.
- `Principal` is resolved by Spring MVC from the security context, so the borrower name comes from the authenticated user and cannot be spoofed in the request body. That is a security decision as much as a design one.
- `POST` returns `201 Created` with a `Location` header, `DELETE` returns `204`, and nothing returns an entity.

Set a ceiling on page size so a client cannot ask for a million rows: `spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size: 100` in `application.yml`.

### One place for errors

Services throw domain exceptions; one `@RestControllerAdvice` converts everything to RFC 9457 `ProblemDetail` JSON. Extending `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` gives correct problem-detail responses for the standard Spring MVC exceptions (malformed JSON, wrong method, missing parameter) for free. We override only the validation case to add field details.

blocks.title: ApiExceptionHandler.java

blocks.text: Typical output of a failed validation (the exact members can vary slightly by version):

blocks.code:
$ curl -s -u librarian:librarian-dev -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"title":"","isbn":"x","authorId":1,"copies":0}' localhost:8080/api/books
{"type":"about:blank","title":"Validation failed","status":400,
 "detail":"Invalid request content.","instance":"/api/books",
 "errors":{"title":"must not be blank","isbn":"must be a valid ISBN",
 "copies":"must be greater than or equal to 1"}}
blocks.title: Typical output
Watch out
blocks.text: Do not add a catch-all `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` to this advice without thought. It would also catch Spring Security's `AccessDeniedException` thrown by method security and turn a correct 403 into a 500. Leave unexpected errors to Boot's default error handling, which returns a generic 500 without a stack trace (the default for `server.error.include-stacktrace` is `never`), and log the real cause server-side.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Security failures raised by the filter chain (401, 403 on URL rules) happen before MVC, so this advice never sees them; they come back with an empty body. That is acceptable for an API; if you want JSON bodies there, supply a custom `AuthenticationEntryPoint` and `AccessDeniedHandler`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Controllers translate: bind and validate input, call one service method, choose the status code.
- Throw domain exceptions in the service; map them centrally in one `@RestControllerAdvice` using `ProblemDetail`.
- Never take identity from the request body when the security context knows it.
- Return DTOs, `201` plus `Location` on create, `204` on delete.

### Roles with HTTP Basic

Two users live in memory, and their passwords come from configuration (so they are environment variables in Compose). This is fine for a learning project; a real system would load users from a database or delegate to an identity provider, as the security chapter described.

blocks.title: SecurityProps.java
SecurityConfig.java

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- Order is everything. The public `GET` rule comes before the librarian rule for the same paths; swap them and nobody could browse anonymously. The final `anyRequest().authenticated()` covers `POST /api/loans` and `GET` `/api/loans/mine` for any logged-in user.
- CSRF is disabled because the API is stateless and uses a header credential, the justification from the security chapter, not a shortcut.
- A user who is logged in but lacks the role gets `403`; no credentials gives `401`.
- Passwords are encoded with BCrypt once at start-up. There is no plain-text password in the code, only configurable defaults for development.

### Web-layer test

`@WebMvcTest` starts only the MVC slice: the controller, the advice and the security filter chain, with services replaced by mocks. It runs in well under a second per test class once the context is cached.

blocks.title: BookControllerTest.java

blocks.text: Records give `BookRequest` a value-based `equals`, which is why `when(service.create(new BookRequest(...)))` matches the deserialised request. These six tests check routing, JSON, validation, error mapping and the security rules, all without a database.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: In Spring Boot 4 the slice annotations moved into feature-specific packages (for example `WebMvcTest` is under `org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure`) and need the matching test starter. `@MockitoBean`, `MockMvc` and `@WithMockUser` are unchanged. Let your IDE fix the imports.

### Service unit test

The business rule is tested with plain JUnit and Mockito: no Spring context at all, so it runs in milliseconds.

blocks.title: LoanServiceTest.java

blocks.text: A natural third layer is a repository test with `@DataJpaTest` against PostgreSQL in Testcontainers (covered in the testing chapter): it would prove the Flyway migration and the derived queries work together. We omit it here so the suite needs no Docker daemon.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Security rules are ordered; public reads first, role rules next, `anyRequest().authenticated()` last.
- Test authorisation explicitly: 401 without login, 403 with the wrong role, success with the right one.
- `@WebMvcTest` plus `@MockitoBean` tests the HTTP contract quickly; plain Mockito tests the business rules even faster.
- Inject time (`Clock`) so tests are deterministic.

### Dockerfile and Compose

Use the multi-stage `Dockerfile` from the shipping chapter unchanged (it builds the jar inside the image). The Compose file runs PostgreSQL and the application, passing credentials as environment variables, which relaxed binding maps to the `${...}` placeholders and properties in `application.yml`:

blocks.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: library
      POSTGRES_USER: library
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-library}
    volumes:
      - dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U library -d library"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

  api:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      DB_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/library
      DB_USER: library
      DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-library}
      LIBRARIAN_PASSWORD: ${LIBRARIAN_PASSWORD:-librarian-dev}
      MEMBER_PASSWORD: ${MEMBER_PASSWORD:-member-dev}
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

volumes:
  dbdata:
blocks.title: docker-compose.yml
Build and start everything

blocks.text:
Without Docker you can run just the database (`docker compose up -d db`) and start the app from your IDE or with `./mvnw spring-boot:run`; the `localhost` defaults in `application.yml` then apply.

### A curl walk-through

The responses below are typical output; ids and dates will differ. First, a librarian creates an author and a book:

blocks.code:
$ curl -s -u librarian:librarian-dev -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"name":"Frank Herbert"}' localhost:8080/api/authors
{"id":1,"name":"Frank Herbert"}
$ curl -s -u librarian:librarian-dev -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"title":"Dune","isbn":"978-0441172719","authorId":1,"copies":1}' \
    localhost:8080/api/books
{"id":1,"title":"Dune","isbn":"978-0441172719","authorId":1,"authorName":"Frank Herbert",
 "copiesAvailable":1,"copiesTotal":1}
blocks.title: Create an author and a book (typical output)

blocks.text: Anyone can browse; a member borrows the only copy; a second attempt conflicts:

blocks.title: Browse, borrow, conflict (typical output)

blocks.text: And the permission checks, printing only the status code:

blocks.code:
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST localhost:8080/api/books
401
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -u alice:member-dev localhost:8080/api/loans
403
$ curl -s -u librarian:librarian-dev -X POST localhost:8080/api/loans/1/return
{"id":1,"bookId":1,"bookTitle":"Dune","borrower":"alice","loanedAt":"2026-03-01",
 "dueDate":"2026-03-15","returnedAt":"2026-03-01"}
blocks.title: Authorisation checks (typical output)

blocks.text:
If every call returns 401, check that the passwords you pass match the ones the container received, and remember that changing the environment requires recreating the container. If the application fails at start with a Flyway or schema validation error, the database volume probably holds an older schema: `docker compose down -v` removes it (and its data).

### Extension ideas

Pick the ones that match what you want to learn.

- Replace the in-memory users with an `AppUser` table, a registration endpoint and a database-backed `UserDetailsService`.
- Switch to JWT: run Keycloak in Compose and turn the API into a resource server.
- Add a `GET /api/loans/overdue` endpoint with a JPQL query, and a scheduled job (`@Scheduled`) that logs overdue loans.
- Add a `@DataJpaTest` with Testcontainers PostgreSQL for the repositories and the Flyway migration.
- Add a Micrometer counter for loans created and expose `prometheus`.
- Add OpenAPI documentation with springdoc and a `v1` path prefix for versioning.
- Add a Redis cache for book searches and measure the difference.
- Add a members table, limits on concurrent loans per member, and a 422 response when the limit is hit.
- Deploy it to a free-tier container platform and add the URL to your CV and README.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: A small, finished, tested and containerised project with a clear README (how to run, endpoint table, design decisions, how to run the tests) is worth more in an interview than a large unfinished one. Be ready to explain each choice: why DTOs, why optimistic locking, why 409 and not 400, why CSRF is disabled.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- A project is finished when someone else can clone it and run it with one command.
- Docker Compose ties the app and PostgreSQL together; configuration enters through environment variables.
- Walk the API with curl, checking 401, 403, 404 and 409 as well as the happy path.
- Keep a README and a list of design decisions; they are what you talk about in interviews.
#### Plan and scaffold

items.question: Why is `spring.jpa.open-in-view` set to `false`, and what does that force you to do?
items.answer: It stops the persistence session from staying open during view rendering, which avoids hidden lazy queries and long connection use. You must finish loading data (and map to DTOs) inside the service transaction.

items.question: What does `${DB_URL:jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/library}` do?
items.answer: It uses the environment variable `DB_URL` if set, otherwise the literal default after the colon.

items.question: You need a new column next week. Do you edit `V1__init.sql`?
items.answer: No. Flyway checksums applied migrations and refuses to start if one changed. Add `V2__add_column.sql`.

items.question: Why does the layout forbid controllers from using entities?
items.answer: Entities are persistence details with lazy relationships; exposing them couples the API to the schema and risks lazy-loading errors and accidental data leaks.

blocks.text: #### Domain, repository and service

items.question: In `update`, there is no `books.save(book)`. Why does the change still reach the database?
items.answer: The entity is managed in an open transaction, so Hibernate dirty-checks it and flushes an `UPDATE` at commit.

items.question: What would break if `LoanService.borrow` caught the `ConflictException` and returned `null`?
items.answer: The transaction would commit with the decremented counter but no loan, silently corrupting the data. Throwing an unchecked exception triggers rollback.

items.question: Why are entity setters avoided here?
items.answer: Changes go through intention-revealing methods that enforce rules (`checkOut`), so invalid states are hard to create.

items.question: The read-only method `mine` calls `this.borrow(...)`, which has its own read-write `@Transactional`. Which settings apply to `borrow`?
items.answer: The caller's read-only transaction. Self-invocation bypasses the Spring proxy, so the annotation on `borrow` is ignored for that call.

items.question: What problem do the `@EntityGraph` annotations prevent?
items.answer: N+1: one query for the list plus one per row to lazy-load the author or book.

blocks.text: #### REST layer with validation and error handling

items.question: Which status does the API return when you `POST` a book with an ISBN that already exists, and which layer decides it?
items.answer: `409 Conflict`; `BookService.create` throws `ConflictException` and the advice maps it.

items.question: Why is the borrower taken from `Principal` instead of the request body?
items.answer: Anything in the body can be forged. The authenticated principal is trustworthy, so a member cannot borrow in someone else's name.

items.question: What is wrong with returning the `Book` entity from the controller (name two problems)?
items.answer: Lazy-loading errors outside a transaction (with open-in-view off), and coupling the public JSON contract to the database schema, which can also leak internal fields. Also risk of infinite recursion on bidirectional relations.

items.question: A client sends malformed JSON. Which code path handles it in this project?
items.answer: `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` (the parent class) handles `HttpMessageNotReadableException` and returns a 400 `ProblemDetail`.

blocks.text: #### Security and tests

items.question: A member calls `GET /api/loans` and receives a response. What status, and which line of `SecurityConfig` decides it?
items.answer: `403 Forbidden`, from `.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/loans").hasRole("LIBRARIAN")` (the member is authenticated but lacks the role).

items.question: Why does `createAsMemberIs403` need `@WithMockUser` while `getBookIsPublic` does not?
items.answer: The first needs an authenticated user to get past authentication to authorisation; the public `GET` rule permits everyone.

items.question: What would the test `invalidBodyIs400WithFieldErrors` fail on if `ApiExceptionHandler` did not override `handleMethodArgumentNotValid`?
items.answer: The `$.errors.title` path: the default response has status 400 but no per-field `errors` property.

items.question: Why does `LoanServiceTest` pass a fixed `Clock`?
items.answer: So "today" is fixed and the due date can be asserted exactly instead of depending on when the test runs.

blocks.text: #### Run it and call it

items.question: In Compose, why is the database URL `jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/library` rather than `localhost`?
items.answer: Inside the API container `localhost` is the container itself; services reach each other by service name on the Compose network.

items.question: You changed `LIBRARIAN_PASSWORD` in your shell but the running container still accepts the old one. Why?
items.answer: Environment variables are fixed when a container is created. Recreate it with `docker compose up -d` `--force-recreate api`.

items.question: A logged-in client calls `/api/book/1` and gets 404. What is the likely mistake?
items.answer: The path is `/api/books/1` (plural); there is no mapping for `/api/book/1`.

items.question: What does `docker compose down -v` do that `down` does not?
items.answer: It also deletes the named volumes, so the database starts empty next time.
